planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown ferns in spring into humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; southern lady fern is the warm-climate counterpart of northern lady fern, thriving through hot, humid Gulf South summers.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; southern lady fern forms graceful, finely divided, lacy fronds in a loose, upright vase-shaped clump that softens the base of trees, shady borders, and woodland gardens throughout the warm, humid Southeast. It is more heat tolerant than the more northern-ranging Athyrium filix-femina, holding good color and texture through Gulf Coast summer humidity that causes many other ferns to decline. New fiddleheads emerge a soft, sometimes reddish green in spring and unfurl quickly into the season's full flush of foliage, which dies back to the crown with the first hard frost. Divide congested crowns every three to four years in early spring, and keep soil consistently moist, especially during dry spells, since this fern does not tolerate extended drought.

planting.note: Tie or wire a small rhizome mat onto rough tree bark, a live oak limb, or a piece of driftwood in dappled shade rather than planting in soil; resurrection fern is a true epiphyte that takes root in bark crevices and accumulated leaf litter, not garden soil.

directions: Attach a small rhizome mat to rough-barked tree limbs, old stumps, or shaded rockwork with twine or wire until it takes hold, rather than planting in soil; resurrection fern grows naturally as a carpet of small, dark green fronds along the limbs of live oaks and other rough-barked trees throughout the Southeast. During drought the fronds curl tightly, shrivel, and turn a dry, dead-looking gray-brown, appearing completely dead for weeks or months, then uncurl and turn lush green again within hours of a soaking rain, the dramatic transformation that gives the plant its common name. It needs no soil, fertilizer, or regular watering once established on a suitable perch, drawing moisture and nutrients from rain, humidity, and accumulated organic debris in bark crevices. This resilience makes it an excellent low-maintenance curiosity for humid Gulf Coast gardens, mounted on tree limbs, arbors, or naturalistic bark-and-rock features.

planting.note: Plant divisions, or detach and root the small plantlets that form on mature fronds, in spring into humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; mother fern propagates unusually easily from its own frond-borne baby plants.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; mother fern produces finely divided, arching, lacy fronds notable for the small plantlets, or bulbils, that form directly on the upper surface of mature fronds and can be detached, once they have a few tiny roots and leaves, and pressed onto moist potting mix to grow into new independent ferns. This viviparous habit makes it one of the easiest ferns to propagate and share, needing no spore culture or division of the crown. In frost-free gardens it forms a full, fountain-like clump that works well in shaded borders, under trees, or in large containers, and it also thrives as a houseplant in bright, indirect light and consistent humidity where winters are too cold for it outdoors. Keep soil evenly moist and humidity high, since dry air causes browning frond tips, and remove old, tattered fronds at the base to keep the clump looking fresh.

planting.note: Wedge a small division into the fibrous boot bases of a cabbage palm trunk, a mounted piece of bark, or a hanging basket of coarse, well-drained epiphytic mix in humid, deep shade; shoestring fern grows naturally as an epiphyte and resents standing in wet soil.

directions: Mount divisions on the fibrous trunk boots of a cabbage palm, a piece of rough bark, or a basket of coarse, fast-draining epiphytic mix in deep, humid shade; shoestring fern is a distinctive Florida and Gulf Coast native epiphyte with long, narrow, grass-like fronds that hang and drape rather than growing upright, giving the plant its descriptive common name. It grows naturally tucked into the boots left by old palm frond bases on live cabbage palms, drawing moisture from humid air, rainfall, and decomposing organic debris rather than soil. Provide consistent humidity and dappled to deep shade, misting during dry spells if grown away from its preferred palm-trunk habitat, and avoid any planting medium that stays soggy, which quickly rots the fine roots. It is an excellent choice for mounting on palm trunks, in hanging baskets, or in a humid greenhouse or lanai setting throughout its frost-free range.

planting.note: Tuck divisions into rock crevices or very well-drained, gritty, alkaline soil in full sun to partial shade; woolly lip fern is one of the most drought-tolerant true ferns, native to dry limestone bluffs and rock outcrops.

directions: Tuck plants into rock crevices, dry stone walls, or gritty, sharply drained, alkaline soil in full sun to partial shade; woolly lip fern breaks the usual rule that ferns need constant moisture and shade, growing naturally on exposed limestone bluffs, cliffs, and rocky slopes across the central and southern United States. Small, finely divided fronds are covered on the undersides with dense, woolly, grayish-white hairs that reduce water loss and give the foliage a soft, felted texture and appearance. Like resurrection fern, it curls and appears shriveled and dead during extended drought, then re-expands and greens up again within a day or two of rain, an adaptation to its harsh, sun-exposed native habitat. Avoid rich soil, heavy mulch, and regular irrigation, all of which cause crown rot in this uniquely drought-adapted fern, and use it in rock gardens or dry stone features where conventional ferns would fail.
